questions.q: What is a credit spread, and why do people watch it?
questions.a: A credit spread is the extra yield riskier companies pay over the government. When lenders get nervous they demand more, so spreads widen. Credit markets often show stress before stocks do, which makes spreads a useful early warning, though not a perfect one.

Hawkish means leaning toward higher interest rates to fight inflation. Dovish means leaning toward lower rates. A central bank that holds rates but signals that hikes are possible is said to be holding hawkishly.

questions.q: What is a real yield, and why does it matter for gold?
questions.a: A real yield is a bond yield after subtracting expected inflation. Gold pays no interest, so when real yields rise, holding gold costs more in forgone income. That is why gold often falls when real yields climb.

questions.q: How can I tell a rotation from a selloff?
questions.a: In a selloff almost everything falls together, volatility jumps and credit spreads widen. In a rotation, some groups fall while others rise and the broad indexes move less. Check the VIX, credit spreads and whether small caps are rising.
